title: Specify a behavior with BDD
summary: Write Given–When–Then in the team’s language, then bind those sentences to the SUT.
description: A meeting-room story specified in Gherkin before any runner files. Read the story and the collaboration steps below first.

story.heading: The story
paragraphs: The office has one bookable meeting room. Facilities posts remaining seats on a board by the door. Product and QA have already agreed the customer-facing rules in plain language: if a party fits, the reservation is confirmed and the board drops by that many seats; if the party is larger than what is left, the reservation is refused and the board does not change.

Nobody treats a helper name as the source of truth. The sentences are the spec — the same words a facilities lead would say in standup. That is the condition that makes BDD worth doing: someone outside engineering will read the feature file, the behavior is user-visible and stable, and each step is a domain fact (party size, seats free, confirmed or refused).

This is not the checkout-coupon TDD page. Room reservations live only here. If the only readers will be the people who wrote the step glue, or the examples would encode CSS and URLs, write a unit test or spike instead — Gherkin would be a second copy of the code.

exercise.heading: How BDD is exercised
exercise.intro: The feature file is the shared example. The step files only bind those sentences. Walk this collaboration before opening a runner tab.

steps.title: Agree the examples in the team’s language
steps.body: Write two scenarios on a whiteboard or in room.feature: a party of 4 with 6 seats free is confirmed and 2 remain; a party of 5 with 3 seats free is refused and 3 remain. Facilities should be able to read both without seeing reserveRoom().

steps.title: Challenge the wording
steps.body: Ask whether “confirmed” and “refused” are the words the board uses. If product wants “booked” instead, change the feature — do not hide a synonym in the glue. The feature stays the source of truth.

steps.title: Watch the runner fail on missing steps
steps.body: Run Cucumber or pytest-bdd against the feature before the glue exists. Undefined steps are the red bar for BDD: the examples are real, the binding is not.

steps.title: Bind Given / When / Then only
steps.body: Map “N seats are free” and “a party of N” to data, “I reserve the room” to one function call, and “confirmed / refused / N seats remain” to assertions. No CSS, no URLs, no helper names in the feature.

steps.title: Grow the function until the feature is green
steps.body: Implement reserveRoom() so both scenarios pass. If a new rule appears (“VIP always fits”), add a scenario to the feature first — do not only patch the function.

steps.title: When to stop
steps.body: Stop when Gherkin would only clone unit-test rows, when no one outside engineering will review the file, or when you are about to automate a UI path you have not agreed on in words. BDD proves the examples the team signed, not every branch of the helper.

architecture: One Gherkin feature is the specification. Each variant only supplies step glue that calls reserveRoom() / reserve_room() in-process (no browser, no HTTP). Conditions that make it effective: shared vocabulary, examples as the source of truth, and steps that hide implementation.

variants.label: Cucumber.js
variants.notes: The feature file is the spec. The step file only binds sentences to reserveRoom().

variants.label: pytest-bdd
variants.notes: Same room.feature as Cucumber.js. Uses pytest-bdd step fixtures when installed; otherwise pytest reads the same Gherkin examples.
